speechtext:
ANOTHER STANLEY CUP FOR LES CANADIENS!-MOTION UNDER
5.0.	43

Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity. Considering that on Thursday, May 25, the Canadiens won a brilliant victory and once again carried off the Stanley Cup, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That congratulations be sent to the directors, coach and players for their success and for the fine way in which they contributed to the prestige of Canada in the world of hockey, where their fame is proverbial.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INDIVIDUAL INVESTMENT IN UNITED STATES-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter or urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43. During Tuesday's debate on my motion calling for a special committee to be established to examine how our federal tax system is forcing Canadian businessmen to invest in the United States, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), in disagreeing with the motion, severely criticized Canadians who choose to invest in the United States and those who have moved there to escape excessive taxation and government regulation.
In view of the hon. member's conviction that Canadians who invest in or move to the United States are greedy, venal and less than loyal to their country, and in view of the startling fact revealed by my colleague, the hon. member for Halton-Went-worth (Mr. Kempling), to the effect that this same member has or had property and business interests in the United
States, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt):
That this House instruct the NDP House leader, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, to ask the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge to explain to the House why it is legitimate for him to have or to have had investments in the United States, but illegitimate, greedy and venal for other Canadians to have similar investments in that country.

subsubtopic: ADVERTISING TO REDUCE ABUSE OF SYSTEM-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion concerns the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has virtually admitted in committee that the recent $3 million advertising campaign against UIC cheating was designed to manipulate the Canadian people into believing that the commission was doing a good job. In view of the fact that this is not the first instance of the use of taxpayers' money by a public agency to manipulate the public politically and to pressure parliament, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That this House condemns the use of taxpayers' money for partisan political purposes by agencies such as the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the Export Development Corporation, the Anti-Inflation Board and Petro-Canada, to name only a few, and notes that if the UIC had really wanted to discourage cheating it could have circulated warnings against it inside envelopes mailed to UIC recipients.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. That this House instructs the Minister of Transport to undertake emergency action which will permit temporary dredging while the department awaits new tenders for permanent work, delayed last year through a technical error in awarding a contract for this project.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION IN ONTARIO LABOUR DISPUTE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that violence on the picket line at the Fleck manufacturing plant in Centralia is increasing, with the reported beating of men and women on the picket line by members of the Ontario provincial police, and in view of the fact that no progress is being made between members of the UAW and the management of the Fleck plant, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent):
That this House instruct the Minister of Labour to approach the premier of Ontario to encourage the management of Fleck to bargain in good faith and reduce the possibility of further violence on the picket line.

subsubtopic: RELEASE OF TASCHEREAU PAPERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgency concerning the so-called Taschereau papers on national security that were scheduled to be made public in 1976 and
May 26, 1978

were removed from the Public Archives prior to such revelation by Major P. A. Lemieux of the Privy Council office. Recently I was informed they were returned to the archives on February 6, 1978, without public knowledge, and a further mandatory term of ten years applied before release, with a review to take place at that time. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That the Prime Minister release all details as to why Michael Pitfield, secretary to the cabinet, wrote a letter to the Public Archives ordering release extension to 1986; all reasons why the Prime Minister and the security committee of the cabinet ordered that such release be delayed; specifically, why it is considered necessary to protect the identity and testimony of certain public servants, some of whom have or are presently occupying high positions in the public service after so many years; and, finally, whether release of such evidence would be incriminating against some of the persons involved.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SCRUTINY OF REAL GROWTH FORECASTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion concerns the fall in real domestic product of 0.2 per cent in March. In view of the fact that this tends to undermine what little credibility remains in the Minister of Finance's 1978 growth target of 5 per cent, and in view of the fact that the minister has yet to make an accurate forecast during his entire career as finance minister, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies):
That this motion does not call upon the Minister of Finance for yet another bogus forecast, but demands that the minister now open his forecasting procedures to public scrutiny and that a special committee of this House be given the mandate to investigate the Department of Finance's forecasting practices.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister, and it relates directly and exclusively to the way in which ministers of the Crown carry out or have carried out their responsibility to uphold the law of Canada.
As hon. members and the minister know, there was a 1972 agreement between the Department of National Revenue and the RCMP which allowed a violation of confidentiality of tax files. The McDonald royal commission yesterday heard testimony to the effect that there was a letter from a minister of national revenue, unidentified, to a solicitor general, unidentified, in which the minister of national revenue expressed the view that that agreement was against the law-that it broke the law of Canada.
I presume that the Deputy Prime Minister, having had his attention drawn to that testimony of yesterday, would have looked into this question. I would like him to tell us whether there was such a letter, whether he will table it, and what was the resolution of the position of the minister of national revenue that the 1972 agreement broke the law of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question of the Leader of the Opposition, I think I should make it clear that so far as I am aware there was no testimony, in the proper sense, put before the commission. As I understand it, there was a reference by commission counsel to a letter, and that was the extent of the proceeding.
In so far as the government is concerned, the matter is before the commission and it is not the intention of the government, as has been stated on many previous occasions, to replace the work of the royal commission. If this letter is to be adduced as evidence, then it ought to be done at the royal commission. That is the place for any other evidence or evidence from ministers, in our view.

Mr. Speaker, once again we have had the capacity of the McDonald royal commission expanded and expanded to cover up activities of this government. Apparently what we have here, according to a letter to which reference was made at that commission yesterday, is an indication that a view was expressed perhaps two years ago by a member of the cabinet of Canada that a practice approved by the cabinet of Canada was against the law. Surely, if the cabinet of Canada is condoning and accepting the breaking of the law of Canada, that is a matter for the House of Commons to inquire into.

Hear, hear!

May 26, 1978
Oral Questions

Was there an expression of a department position by a minister that an agreement sanctioned by the Government of Canada was in violation of the law of Canada? Was there such a letter? If so, can the House of Commons, to which this government reports-royal commission or no-see that letter? Can the minister tell us whether it continues to be the policy of the Government of Canada to support the breaking of the law of Canada?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think as the hon. Leader of the Opposition built his question he drew additional and unwarranted conclusions. As I understand it, what happened yesterday was that commission counsel made brief reference to a letter which had been exchanged and put a particular construction upon the letter himself.
Let's see the letter.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no desire on the part of the government to impede the work of the royal commission in any sense.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As far as we are concerned, we would be very pleased to have this matter fully, thoroughly and expeditiously examined before the royal commission, have whatever evidence is available put on the record, have whatever ministers may be involved in the transmission of correspondence examined before the commission, and have all the evidence brought forward. Certainly, it is not the intention of the government to replace the royal commission, nor is it the intention of the government to put on the record of the House of Commons fragments of information. I think that would be quite irresponsible and quite opposed to the work of the McDonald royal commission.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, no one has ever accused this government of trying to impede the work of the royal commission. It is attempting to use the royal commission to impede the work of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

If the Deputy Prime Minister is worried about unwarranted interpretations of a letter from one of his colleagues to another alleging that the Government of Canada was breaking the law, the way he can resolve those concerns is to let us see the letter. If it continues to be the view of the Minister of National Revenue that that agreement is illegal, can he tell us if he has received a legal opinion from the Minister of Justice as to whether that matter is legal or illegal? He can come clean by telling us what the government of Canada is authorizing, whether it is authorizing activities which violate the law of Canada, and stop trying to hide behind a royal commission.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is not authorizing activities which are against the law of Canada, nor is the Government of Canada attempting to hide behind the McDonald royal commission. It was as a result of repeated representations from members of the opposition that this government finally agreed to establish the McDonald royal commission.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Finally.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This was because it had been stated frequently that the subject matter which was the concern of the House of Commons was not an appropriate subject for the House of Commons and it ought to be dealt with by the McDonald royal commission. That is why we established the McDonald royal commission.
I want to repeat precisely the same position that was taken by the government on previous occasions when the credibility of witnesses was under examination by the House and when contradictory evidence was put forward before the royal commission and hon. members asked questions in the House. I believe the place to conclude all these questions is before the McDonald commission, where all the evidence will come out in context.
After the election.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. leader of the NDP says "After the election". That shows the suspicious mind he has.
You want to believe it.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Maybe the hon. member should have had the foresight not to advocate the establishment of a royal commission if he felt its work might not coincide with his electoral objectives.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What he wants to do, of course, is use this issue for political purposes and not to obtain the truth which we believe will be forthcoming at the McDonald royal commission, not through the politicking of members of the opposition.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I have a question for the expert on parliamentary government in this House, the Deputy Prime Minister. Since he, of all people, knows that the central characteristic of parliamentary government is cabinet responsibility to members of this House, if he were interested in the truth, instead of obscuring it, he would realize that the government's central obligation, in view of this political decision reached by the cabinet, is to produce the letter that has been demanded by members on this side.
Considering it is now part of the evidence submitted to the royal commission, that the man who was superintendent of the legal branch of the RCMP, Mr. J. V. Cain, submitted to his superior a memo dated March 3 of this year and in the view of
Oral Questions
the expert in the RCMP the agreement that had been reached and authorized by the cabinet in 1972 was legal, I would like to ask if he will confirm that the cabinet authorized this agreement in 1972. Will he also inform the House whether or not there was an opinion offered by the minister of justice at that time on the legality of this agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I confirm that the agreement was entered into in 1972. My recollection is, subject to checking, that it was a matter approved by the cabinet and there is absolutely no suggestion or evidence that the agreement was in any way illegal.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if it is the minister's view that it was not illegal-and he has at least offered his opinion on this matter that is before the McDonald inquiry-will he not reconsider the position he took just a minute ago and provide for all the members of this House and the people of Canada, well in advance of the final report of the royal commission, the letter in question so that we will have an opportunity to judge the opinion that was offered allegedly by one minister of the Crown on this important matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. member, who is normally fair-minded, would understand how dangerous it would be to produce one single element of the total evidence that will be brought before the royal commission. What happened yesterday was that reference was made by commission counsel to a letter upon which he placed a particular construction. I am not commenting one way or the other on the validity of that construction; but surely, if the letter is relevant, it ought to be considered in the over-all context of all the evidence. If a minister of the Crown is involved in the writing of the letter, then he ought to be heard before the commission and his evidence sought, so that the commission and those who are following the commission can reach a proper conclusion.
It seems to me that it would be a very wrong practice to feed into the House of Commons, in response to newspaper accounts, bits and pieces of evidence and expect that the matter would be dealt with other than in a highly partisan and highly political way.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one institution in Canada in which politics should be thoroughly discussed, surely it is the House of Commons. Considering that this matter, the decision that was made in 1972 and the subsequent testimony before the royal commission pertaining to the decision, is the first clear indication that the government abused its legal authority in condoning illegal activity, and since those allegations are clearly out now, does the Deputy Prime Minister not agree that the cabinet has a primary political responsibility in this case not to wait for the findings of the royal commission, but to help clear the air now, well in advance of the next election, so the people of Canada can judge in a fair-minded way whether the cabinet has performed legally or illegally?

May 26, 1978
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL

Mr. Speaker, as I have stated already, the ministers have already indicated their intention to appear before the royal commission. They can be summoned at any moment the commission so decides and this particular aspect can be dealt with thoroughly and expeditiously long before the election which the hon. member fears so much.
The hon. member says the House of Commons is the place for politics. I agree with him. If we are to take the views of the opposition seriously, however, it is not the place to deal with the activities of the RCM Police in order to determine what illegalities may have occurred-

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: It is the cabinet we are talking about.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FORMER REVENUE MINISTER AND SOLICITOR GENERAL

My hon. friend again forgets that it was at the request of members of the opposition that we put this whole problem before the McDonald royal commission. Now, when there is a snippet of information that may have dribbled out of the commission, the opposition wants to bring it before the House of Commons for political purposes.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the first thing we should do is get back to the original question asked by the Leader of the Opposition, which is simply this: Was there such a letter in which the Government of Canada was found guilty in advance of doing what was wrong and illegal? Is there such a letter?
I have followed the hon. gentleman's circumlocution with interest and with admiration for his political adroitness, but we come back to the question: Did the Government of Canada know that what was being done was illegal, unlawful and unjustifiable according to the opinion of the Department of Justice? That is all. If so, where is the letter? The fact that the minister has evaded the whole problem so well and so cleverly could lead even the least suspicious to conclude that the reason he is doing it is to hide the facts. They do not want to be found guilty of wrongdoing as was the opinion of a lawyer in the Department of Justice.
This is a very serious matter and not one for a royal commission; it is for parliament to determine. Will the minister produce the document? If there is nothing in it, there will be nothing to worry about; but if there is, he knows there will be a problem for the government.

I think there is reason to applaud the initiative of the committee and group promoting Mirabel and its usefulness for passengers and cargo as a developmental place. I am rather happy that they decided to use the white elephant symbol. I know they will have a great deal of help from the opposition in drawing attention to the symbol over a period of time and that will, no doubt, reinforce their campaign.

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the minister approves of the ad. While some people may applaud the ad and the operation of the airport, I can assure him and you, sir, that the taxpayers of Canada are not applauding the airport nor the ad.
I ask the minister if he is disregarding the comments of the international association of pilots. Does he not think the orange star, which in their view rates it as a deficient airport in terms of safety, should be taken into consideration, or does he not agree with their assessment? If he does not agree, is he going to take immediate steps to make sure that assessment is clarified? It seems to me the pilots are the logical people to assess the safety or otherwise of an airport.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought I had put the matter into perspective for the hon. member by indicating the ambulance response time. It is true that the location of Mirabel means it takes longer for ambulances to arrive than it does from the downtown centres of some of the smaller towns and cities nearby. There is a longer time-span for a large number of ambulances to arrive at Mirabel. On the other hand, Mirabel, unlike most airports, has a 24-hour ambulance service available, which has been used.
I think there is room for disagreement about the type of service that should be provided. I simply point out that I do not in any way diminish the view of the pilots about how they would like all conditions to be ideal, in an ideal world. This is a very small element compared to some of the elements they have noted at other airports with which red and black stars have been associated. Yet aircraft fly into those airports in great numbers. It is a relative matter that we have to weigh against all the other expenditures we could make in terms of air safety. I come back again to the over-all situation, which is that in allocating funds for air safety in Canada we have managed to produce about the safest civil aviation system in the world.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister: it follows from questions put by the right hon. member for Prince Albert and the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Like a criminal.

subtopic: WAYS AND MEANS INCOME TAX AND EXCISE TAX

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Finance) moved:
subtopic: WAYS AND MEANS INCOME TAX AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext: That the ways and means motion to amend the Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act laid upon the table, Thursday, May 25,1978, be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.

The House resumed, from Thursday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-56, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole, and of the amendment (Mr. Broadbent) (p. 5548).

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak in this debate today. I should like to restrict my remarks to the budget. This is one of the measures I consider to be one of the most important that the Government of Canada has ever initiated because I think it tries to answer two main challenges in this country. The first challenge is the economy. If we had a plan to propose to the Canadian people to reduce prices for the shopper, to stimulate sales for the storekeeper, to encourage use of savings, to boost manufacturing indirectly, and to give an over-all boost to the economy, including reducing inflation which is the underlying factor in the whole set of our economic problems, we would probably all accept it eagerly.
Income Tax Act
Our second challenge is federal-provincial cooperation where there is a new thrust as part of our whole national unity picture, where admittedly we have problems in such a big country with strong and varied regional interests, with cyclical changes throughout our history in terms of centralized versus regional power, with the present trend toward increasing provincial power but still with a need for a strong central government in the interests of national unity, international competitiveness, fairness and equity across the country. Certainly with regard to these two challenges, the economy and federal-provincial co-operation, this is the sort of promise held out by at least one recent Government of Canada initiative in the last budget, namely, the proposed retail sales tax cut announced in the April budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
As we know, this type of tax cut, novel in our history, was agreed to in general at the federal-provincial economic summit conference in February, here in Ottawa. It was recommended before that, and since then, by many prominent economists in this country, and it seemed to have the general agreement of all the provinces except Quebec which delayed its decision until after the budget announcement and then, to the surprise of many of us, bucked the deal, which we can only interpret as typical separatist tactics.

When you add that to what has already been provided in the budget by the province of Saskatchewan, $18 million to $82 million, our province's contribution to stimulating our economy and creating more employment amounts to $100 million.
I want to quote our Saskatchewan minister of finance. He said:
I want to say that our preference would have been for a permanent federal income tax reduction for low and middle income Canadians. That would have
put cash into the hands of those who need it most and surely would have stimulated consumer spending on an on-going basis.
We have requested in the House for many months that a $1.5 billion cut in personal income taxes be made to do that very thing. Saskatchewan accepted, as a less preferable option, and agreed to cooperate with, the federal government's proposal to have reductions in retail sales taxes. But the Saskatchewan minister of finance also said the following:
I regret that the federal offer to participate in this tax cut came so late. From the standpoint of budget planning, it would have been much better to have known the federal government's intentions well in advance, so that we could have introduced this additional tax cut in our budget on March 7.
A similar quandary applied to many other provinces as well. The Saskatchewan minister of finance went on to say:
Certainly, the finance ministers' meeting in January, or the first ministers' meeting in February, would have provided an ideal forum for the federal government to present such a tax proposal to the provinces. But this did not take place.
If the federal government wishes to bring in a budget whose main thrust is to intervene in a tax area that is solely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, surely it should have had the courtesy, surely it should have felt it a requirement, to discuss it openly and in public view at the meetings of the ministers of finance, or at least at the first ministers' meeting in February, and reach an agreement with the provinces which would have been included in a budget that would be subsequently presented by the federal Minister of Finance.
The government has chosen to hang its hat on its obstinate refusal to change this bill because Quebec's sales tax reduction is somehow going to balkanize our economy, is meant to help Quebec only. That kind of contention that the federal government makes falls in the face of the facts.
I want to quote the minister of finance of Saskatchewan again. He said:
Since last fall, I have been urging the federal government to move to stimulate consumer spending. More spending would gradually put idle plant capacity and the unemployed back to work. The federal government did not agree with this approach. Instead, greater tax concessions were given to industry. Manufacturing plants were encouraged to expand even though 16 per cent of our existing plant capacity was idle.
What sensible owner or operator of a manufacturing plant that is 16 per cent idle is going to spend money to expand that plant? He is just not going to do it if he is a wise and sensible businessman. While the federal government's policies were in place, what has happened? We have had more lay-offs, more shutdowns, and more Canadians out of work.
We submit, and so does the minister of finance in Saskatchewan, that these national economic policies have been misguided.
I want to turn now to a further remark of the minister of finance of Saskatchewan, so that there is no misunderstanding. Even though the Saskatchewan government agreed to cooperate and gave a commitment to reduce our sales tax by 2 per cent for nine months, the minister of finance of that province has also said:
I am concerned that the federal government intruded into an area of provincial jurisdiction by trying to establish policy for the provincial retail sales tax. A

May 26, 1978

dangerous precedent was established when the provinces were not allowed to participate in the formulation of a federal compensation formula which does not apply equally to all provinces.
Mr. Smishek went on to say:
Mr. Speaker, the western premiers made it clear, when they met in Yorkton, that they were not pleased-that the temporary sales tax reduction was not a precedent for future intrusions by the federal government into tax fields traditionally held by the provinces.
Mr. Smishek went on to say:
Let me make clear that I do not rule out-indeed I welcome-federal-provincial co-operation in fiscal matters. But this was the wrong way to go about it.
Let us look at the situation regarding Quebec's entitlement under this budget. I said earlier that our preference, and that of the government of Saskatchewan, was for stimulation to be provided by further reductions in the personal income tax for low and middle income families, which is solely within the jurisdiction of the national government.
There is another option which would be solely within the jurisdiction of the federal government. The federal government should have looked into a reduction in its own sales tax if it wished to implement a sales tax reduction to stimulate the economy. Federal sales tax revenues amount to approximately $4 billion. A federal sales tax reduction, with appropriate legislation and monitoring, could see to it that the benefit was passed from the manufacturers and the wholesalers to the consumers. Perhaps for the first time the Anti-Inflation Board would have been put to some useful work, that is, monitoring the wholesalers and manufacturers to make certain a federal sales tax reduction was passed on to consumers. That option is less preferable than a reduction in income taxes.
Instead, the government chose to intervene in an area which belonged solely to the provinces. With the benefit of hindsight, I am sure provincial officials in many provinces feel they have received a pig in a poke. In any event, some provinces agreed to cooperate, gave commitments, and are living up to them.
I should like to refer to the case of Quebec. According to the figures of the federal government, if Quebec were to reduce its sales tax by 2 per cent across the board it would be entitled to approximately $226 million by way of direct payment, tax room, or whatever. The removal of the 8 per cent sales tax in five areas in Quebec will cost the treasurer of that province $340 million, according to federal government figures. If the Minister of Finance would telephone the Saskatchewan minister of finance, I am sure he would be told to give Quebec the amount to which it is entitled. I am confident that would be the response from Saskatchewan. Also, I have some confidence that many other provinces would say the same thing.
How, when, for how long, and in what amount retail sales taxes are levied, are entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. If one province reduces its retail sales tax by 2 per cent for nine months across the board, and another province reduces its tax by 3 per cent for six months across the board, they have a perfect right to do so. The Minister of Finance recognized and accepted that fact. Equally it is valid for
Income Tax Act
another province to decide to remove taxes totally from certain commodities or areas of sale within its jurisdiction.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have said that Quebec is attempting to balkanize its economy, is selfish, and wants to help itself only. That theory does not hold water.
It is false, when the facts are examined. A sales tax reduction in Quebec of the 8 per cent on shoes, furniture, textiles, clothing, and hotel bills, amounts to a total of $340 million. Quebec's share, whether in the form of tax room or whatever from the federal government, is $226 million. Quebec's removal of sales tax from four of those five areas will benefit Ontario manufacturers more than it will Quebec manufacturers. I see an hon. member opposite is shaking his head. I should like to remind him that the figures pertaining to shoes, furniture, textile and clothing manufacturing, were obtained from Statistics Canada.
Referring to the retail sale of shoes in the province of Quebec, a little over half are manufactured outside Canada; 46 per cent are manufactured in Canada; 23 per cent are manufactured in Ontario; and 20 per cent are manufactured in Quebec. Surely that means the reduction in sales tax on shoes will be of at least as much benefit to Ontario manufacturers and their employees as their counterparts in Quebec. That is hardly balkanization.
Turning to the furniture industry, 88 per cent of its retail sales in Quebec is manufactured in Canada, 35 per cent is manufactured in Quebec, and 44 per cent is manufactured in Ontario. With an increase in consumer spending and purchasing of furniture in Quebec, an equal or larger benefit will result to Ontario furniture manufacturers. That can hardly be called balkanizing the Canadian economy.
The same situation applies to the clothing industry. Approximately 32 per cent of the clothing sold in Quebec is manufactured there, and 37 per cent is manufactured in the province of Ontario. A reduction in sales tax will be of equal or greater benefit to manufacturers and employees in the Ontario clothing industry as it will be in Quebec.
Quebec's decision to remove sales tax will be of benefit mainly to the low and middle income earners. This benefit applies to areas which are essential to them such as shoes, clothing, furniture, yard goods, and ordinary things. It will reduce their cost of living by approximately 8 per cent. If Quebec chooses to do it this way, it has that right. It is in our constitution.
The government and the minister of finance of Saskatchewan have no objection to the Government of Canada reimbursing, in an agreed upon manner, the $226 million to the province of Quebec. The Quebec sales tax reduction amounts to $340 million. The budget proposal has done a great deal of harm to Confederation and has hurt co-operative federalism. No political party or no government is perfect. Any political party or any government can make a mistake. This is a mistake. It will be of no political harm to the Government of Canada and the Minister of Finance if they agree to go back to the provinces, particularly Quebec, to negotiate and arrive at an agreement.

May 26, 1978
Income Tax Act
Approximately an hour ago I had a telephone conversation with the Saskatchewan minister of finance. He indicated that the Minister of Finance should go back and meet with Quebec's minister of finance in order to make arrangements to give Quebec the share it is properly entitled to, the $226 million. In fact, arrangements should be made to give every province that to which they are entitled. How Quebec chooses to reduce sales tax is Quebec's business, just as it is the business of Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia or any other province.
This business of the Minister of Finance trying to set up a budget on the basis of hotel room discussions with successive ministers and premiers, from one day to the next, just a few weeks prior to bringing down the budget, is not good enough. This is not what you could call real consultation. There is no reason this idea could not have been put on the table at the first minister's conference in February. It could have been discussed then, and the nation as a whole could have watched the ten premiers and the Prime Minister negotiating and agreeing to proposals for a national budget and budgets of nine provincial governments, reducing sales tax with federal and provincial cooperation. They could have agreed then on how the reductions would be shared. That did not happen.
The manner in which it has been carried out is just not good enough for at least four western premiers who have indicated their unhappiness about it. They will stick by what they agreed and committed themselves to; they are men of their word. Since the minister put the budget proposal to the province of Quebec and that province chose to reduce its sales tax in a different manner than the other provinces, I do not see why the federal government should think it has a problem. This is accomplishing in a different way what the national government want to see accomplished by its budget, namely, significant reductions in sales tax to increase consumer spending and thereby stimulate economic growth and employment.
The argument is not so much in opposition to what is being done by the federal government, but how it is being done. The federal government is trying to suggest to the provinces, whether they be Quebec, Saskatchewan or others, how they should levy their retail sales tax, something in respect of which the federal government has no business, jurisdiction or authority whatsoever.
It seems to me this government would do well to say it will not call this bill for another two or three weeks, or it will accept the amendment proposed by my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), will go back to the other provinces to work out an agreement, and then come back in a month's time with an amended bill. I am sure the government would then find members on this side of the House ready to see it passed quickly. That is all that is needed.
I would not even expect members of this government to blush; just admit they have made a mistake and are happy to do all they can to correct it, and are willing to do what the Minister of Finance has suggested on previous occasions, namely, negotiate. Surely that would be a sign of real leadership and

statesmanship. Surely that would restore some confidence in cooperative federalism. That would be a move toward national unity instead of playing into the hands of the separatists.
As things stand now those separatists can suggest that, in a tax field that is entirely provincial, Ottawa is trying to interfere, and Confederation is not working for them. In this way the Minister of Finance and the Liberal government have played into the hands of those who want to destroy Confederation.
There are other ways in respect of this bill or a subsequent one in which the government could help Canadians through our present economic difficulties. Let me put forward one suggestion which I know the Prime Minister has received and has said has been turned over to the Minister of Finance for serious consideration.
We require an amendment to our income tax laws that would do away with the standard $100 deduction for charitable contributions. The standard deduction would then only apply in respect of medical expenses. Those who give to charitable or voluntary organizations would get credit in respect of income tax, but only if they actually made contributions. A tax credit of 50 per cent, as has been suggested by voluntary organizations, would be allowed in respect of those contributions. This would encourage even bigger contributions by Canadians to these worthwhile organizations. The Association of Voluntary Organizations in Canada is unanimous in this suggestion, and this includes the Canadian Cancer Society, the YMCA, and a host of others.
An increase in the funding of those organizations would benefit not only those who are the beneficiaries of their activities, but also those who would be hired to staff the organizations in order to carry out additional work. The organizations would then be in a position to do an even better job in communities across this country.
This is a provision which may not look like very much at first blush, but one which would provide the incentive and opportunity for Canadians to do an even better job in helping one another through these voluntary organizations. It would also stop some of those who are now taking advantage of the standard $100 deduction as a credit on income tax without giving a nickel. Let us remove that provision and provide a tax credit for those who now give generously and might then give even more generously.
Such a change would be helpful and useful to the communities in Canada. It would encourage people to work together even more than they now are, and would be a symbol or a sign of how this parliament and this government are making significant efforts toward fostering national unity and cooperative federalism.
I began my remarks by saying we are not going to assist this government to precipitate the suicide of our Confederation. I do not care if Liberals want to commit suicide, but we are not going to offer that kind of assistance. I hope members opposite will accept our amendment. I plead with them to return to the finance ministers of Quebec and the other nine provinces for

May 26, 1978

consultation, and then to come back to this House in two weeks or a month with a new bill. We would be agreeable, even though this meant sitting a few days in July. Such a new bill would confirm that Quebec, like the other provinces, has the right to levy sales tax in whatever manner it wishes, because this is solely within provincial jurisdiction.
Quebec as well as the other provinces would then get the money or the tax room to which they have a right under the federal government's new proposal. Quebec is entitled to $225 million and it should receive that amount. We do not need this sleazy idea of paying $85 to each income taxpayer in Quebec. This is another thing that will harm Confederation and play into the hands of the separatists. This is a typical Jimmy Gardiner trick, and it will not wash.
The government must admit it has made a mistake, and if it does so it will be applauded. The government must come back with an amended bill. It will get the support from all sides of the House and it will reinforce what is the constitution of Canada, the jurisdictions of the national government and the provinces in various tax areas. It will weaken the argument of those who would break up our confederation and who say that it does not work. It is a positive contribution. I say for my province of Saskatchewan that the government would have the full support and co-operation from us in that kind of endeavour. The minister of finance of Saskatchewan has said "Give Quebec the amount they are entitled to by whatever method you agree on, $225 million. They get no more, no less, than any other province."
Quebec is doing this differently. Well, so is Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Ontario, and the Atlantic provinces. Whether it is tax cuts across the board or tax cuts on certain commodities, it is the business of the provinces. When are my good friends on the government side going to admit they have made a mistake, that there was not sufficient consultation and that all of this could have been arrived at and agreed to before the provinces brought down their budgets? All of this could have been arrived at and agreed to by the time the Minister of Finance brought down his budget in this parliament.
I beg the government, Mr. Speaker, not to proceed in the manner in which they presently intend. It will only do harm and it can easily be avoided. Here is an opportunity where they can show some leadership and statesmanship, and they will get the support of the members on this side of the House as well. I urge the government to accept our proposal, to delay further dealing with this bill until they have returned to the provinces, obtained an amended agreement, and brought back another bill with those amendments. This parliament will deal with it quickly and Canada will be much stronger for it.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with, I also would like to express my support to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for his excellent budget of last April
Income Tax Act
10. And since I believe that this is the right place to express support or disagreement for such a taxation measure which has been making the headlines since April 10, I want to take this opportunity to do so in the House of Commons and shall explain why. In the 40 minutes alloted to me, Mr. Speaker, I shall deal mostly with that most controversial part of the budget which provides for a rebate of provincial taxes, and an obvious problem with this part of the budget is precisely that it has been called the provincial tax rebate.
After long consultations-I do not want to go over all the negotiations which preceded the budget speech on April 10 last-but after long consultations starting in October 1977 and continuing afterwards following the representations made in February and March 1978 by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce according to taxation and economy experts like the C.D. Howe Institute, everyone seemed to agree that the quickest and most direct way to give the Canadian economy the impetus it so urgently needed, was to reduce the sales tax, which comes under provincial jurisdiction. For many years, the provinces have been pressing the Federal government for more participation and a greater say in major fiscal policies, discussions, or decisions. So, in keeping with their requests, in October 1977 all the provinces were consulted, starting with the premiers, down to the ministerial and finally the high executive levels of the provincial departments of finance.
Following the advice of the experts that I referred to earlier, who had supported this tax rebate, and after having figured out the implications in each provincial department involved, provincial authorities have chosen to accept that proposal and cut their taxes for a fixed period to stimulate the economy immediately rather than abolishing a tax permanently. By abolishing or removing a tax for six or nine months, the economists and experts thought that people would be encouraged to make certain expenses earlier, which would stimulate the economy.
While two provinces had some reservations about the Minister of Finance's proposals, some adjustments and arrangements were made to meet their expectations and the previous speaker, my hon. colleague from Regina-Lake Centre comes from one of those provinces, Saskatchewan. Those two provinces expressed some reservations and arrangements were made so that they would join the program. And indeed an arrangement was made to their satisfaction.
The day after the budget we heard from the province of Quebec that this measure would penalize Quebeckers and their industries, that it was again an invasion by the federal government in a provincial jurisdiction when the province was seeking to have more say in the decision making process. However, Quebec remained silent during all those consultations and even during the three weeks preceeding the budget. There was no appeal or counter proposals from the Quebec minister of finance. Of course we should not expect anything else because his party wants to take Quebec out of Canada. So it would not

May 26, 1978
Income Tax Act
be reasonable to expect from them a favourable attitude towards the federal proposals. They are deceitful, Mr. Speaker. They wait until all other provinces accept the project or the proposal because it is fiscally interesting and feasible, easily controled and favourable to all parts of the country without discriminating against any industry.
The day after the introduction, the finance minister stated that he was against the proposal made by the federal government. That is the same man who three years ago, perhaps four, Mr. Speaker-1 forget because it is not my favourite topic- launched a newspaper called Le Jour which failed. Still it was an undertaking conceived, designed and developed by that famous finance minister who is apparently living in a fantasy world. He thinks of himself as a cow watching a train go by. Such was his own admission in the National Assembly in reply to a question put by a member of the opposition. He said: You know of the difficulties in which the Minister of Finance now finds himself; me, I am somewhat like a cow watching a train go by. Perhaps those comments are unparliamentary, Mr. Speaker, but they were uttered by the Quebec finance minister and his description of the situation faithfully mirrors what I think of him.
So the question is whether Quebeckers are really penalized and how a minister who is supposed to be an economist can reach such a conclusion. Mr. Speaker, I would like to consider the impact of the proposal made by the Minister of Finance on the economy and the collection of provincial taxes. I see that the respected member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has not left yet; I wish he would stay a few more minutes, Mr. Speaker, so that he can see the other side, the other way of analyzing this tax cut program.
As I indicated earlier, a 3 per cent tax cut over a period of six months will stimulate purchasing. A number of people will buy certain goods earlier than they expected, for instance to replace carpeting, furnishings, a suit or what have you. However we suggested a six-month cut for those who accepted the scheme and nine months for those who prefer the nine months, without discriminating against any industry, except of course alcoholic beverages, cigarettes and such things.
So this increase which could normally and legitimately be expected would have reduced the loss that the provinces will suffer, will reduce the loss that the provinces expect to have, because if you figure it out, Mr. Speaker, it takes a 14 per cent increase in sales to compensate for the 1 per cent which the provinces will have to pay. Early indications in provinces other than Quebec show that not one province will experience a loss because in fact of this 14 per cent increase in sales that can compensate for the 1 per cent paid by the provinces. So it is not a bad deal.
We are not trying to penalize the industries which are doing well in those provinces, we do not discriminate; as for myself,

Mr. Speaker, I am not altogether convinced that helping only a few industries will lead to economic recovery. I believe that the universal formula of promoting industry is the best, the simplest and the one that offers the most leeway. And I am convinced that on the economic and fiscal levels, helping four industries which perhaps are not doing well-and I have figures, Mr. Speaker, to disprove some arguments of the Quebec finance minister in that regard-that helping four industries is perhaps not the best way to ensure economic recovery in a country or a province. As I indicated a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, a 14 per cent increase in sales of all goods subject to the tax cut will compensate the province for the loss it would have incurred without the increase. We can well expect at least a 14 per cent increase, but more probably closer to 20 per cent. If on the other hand you take away the 8 per cent tax on certain goods, if you remove it completely, there is no way the province can get its money back, even with a 40 per cent increase in sales, which is doubtful. In my view the increase could be limited to approximately 15, 20 or 22 per cent, but even if it were 50 per cent, there is no way the province of Quebec could get the money back on those 8 per cent that were removed. We are talking here of course in the case of the province of Quebec of the 6 per cent on its goods, because 2 per cent will be paid back by the federal government.
That is their business.

The hon. member is suggesting that is their business. When the deal is bad we should not be intimating it is a good one because that is their business.
Mr. Speaker, how is it possible to suggest we should penalize this country's economy, deprive the economy and the Canadian people of several initiatives because of an alleged invasion to a degree of a provincial jurisdiction? My colleague from Regina-Lake Centre suggested earlier that such an invasion by the federal government had not been seen since the war years. But apparently the economic situation was serious at the end of 1977. The first ministers at the federal-provincial conference all expressed a desire to sit down with the federal government and prepare measures to counteract, to put the economy back on the right track, to solve economic difficulties. In those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance candidly trusted all ministers of finance. He was right eight times out of nine, which is not such a bad score. I feel his batting average is excellent.
Of course it is normal that after the fact there is a temptation to suggest this was a federal invasion. But we were opposing this, we only joined the program because they themselves were urging us to do so. There is no need to quote from the multiplicity of speeches that were made on the subject by the majority of Canada's ministers of finance, urging action and inviting the federal government to come up with proposals.

May 26, 1978

Well, they did. The federal government made some proposals and that is how it happened.
But, Mr. Speaker, to give a new impetus to the economy of a country, it is not enough to give help to four industries if we want to make sure that things pick up, especially in view of the dead loss the Quebec government will incur by abolishing the 8 per cent tax in their case, since 2 per cent will be reimbursed by the Canadian government. That loss will amount to something like $120,000, $140,000 or $150,000 depending on the volume of business. The Quebeckers should ask their minister of finance, Mr. Parizeau, to reverse his silly decision and accept the proposal of the federal government in which case there is no loss because, as I said before, and I shall repeat it for those who were not here, an increase of 14 per cent in sales would allow a reimbursement to the province of that 1 per cent loss it will incur by reducing the 4 per cent sales tax as opposed to joining the national program that would reduce it by 5 per cent.
Of course, with the benefit of insight after the fact, Mr. Speaker, it is an easy statement to make: Had we been consulted, we would have liked to study an entirely different proposal. 1 say, Mr. Speaker, that with the results that notorious Minister of Finance has had with the newspaper Le Jour on two occasions with his concept of business, as I said before, he seems to live in a world of fantasy. It is no wonder, Mr. Speaker, that he should have preferred to show off in front of the Quebec population and tell them boldly that he was cancelling the 8 per cent tax on furniture, clothing, shoes and textiles. Of course, it was also an unexpected opportunity for him to be forgiven for having taxed children's clothing. Quebec was probably the only province where children's clothing was taxable. By abolishing the sales tax on clothing, footwear, textiles and furniture, he saw this as an opportunity to be forgiven. And it is true, as the previous speaker said, that most of the furniture sold in the province of Quebec is not manufactured in Quebec but in Ontario. I am convinced that Ontario manufacturers will not gain anything from that; merchants and retail dealers of Quebec are the ones who will benefit from this measure. And following the refusal of the province of Quebec-I should not say the province of the Quebec but its present government-to join in a national fiscal program, I do not think that the public will be prepared to further encourage Quebec manufacturers. And I also think, Mr. Speaker, that this is a discriminatory way to stimulate the economy.
If I lived in the Joliette riding and belonged to the Joliette chamber of commerce, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) would know what I think of Mr. Parizeau's proposal, since there are many corporations in Joliette which cannot benefit from this rebate, and neither can the Bigelow corporation which makes carpets in Sainte-Agathe-des Monts, in my own constituency. And these people are outright insulted by
Income Tax Act
this discriminatory approach to helping Quebec industries and stimulating the economy.
First of all, I am thinking of the unions, of the unionized workers of the Hupp Canada corporation, in l'Assomption, who do not benefit from this rebate, this tax cut, of the employees of Westinghouse in Trois-Rivieres, I should say of the 600 Westinghouse employees in Trois-Rivieres, of the employees of the Raleigh corporation in Waterloo, Drum-mondville, Cowansville or elsewhere in the province of Quebec, who do not benefit from it either. In Saint-Germain, for instance, Pacific Mobile, with 300 workers, is excluded from this tax cut, as are the 700 Lowney's employees in Sherbrooke who are terribly discriminated against because they have not been chosen to benefit under this national program.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, it is only normal that workers who manufacture cans should stage a demonstration in Quebec City because the sales tax on those products is going up by 5 per cent. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, why some unions in the industries I mentioned did not stage any demonstrations in Quebec City to demand that 3 per cent tax cut on their products, which would have allowed the province of Quebec to increase its revenues and to stimulate its economy, without having to suffer a loss in tax receipts for all that, because as I was saying earlier, a 14 per cent increase in sales compensates for this 1 per cent cut.
So, it is quite unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, that the Quebec minister of finance, who is an economist, did not realize that. No wonder, since he was the one who led his fellow citizens in the venture of Le Jour and he is responsible for salary lost by a great number of journalists when this newspaper went bankrupt. There are so many things that could be said on the manner in which the economy of the province of Quebec is managed, Mr. Speaker. We learned recently, we read this week press reports about replies to questions put by the opposition in Quebec City, that members have been calling for the tabling of the Bonin report, a report which has reviewed the economic opportunities of the province of Quebec should it separate, that is the separatist government is bent on proving, by means of well-organized propaganda, that the separation of Quebec could be to the economic advantage of Quebeckers. It is quite an aberration to believe this, but that is what they are dreaming about. So, a high official by the name of Bonin was asked to conduct a study. This study has been completed but Mr. Levesque refuses to table it as his premise that separation was economically favourable for Quebec is disproved in this report. And I would bet my last dollar, Mr. Speaker, that this report will never be tabled.
Instead of selecting four so-called "soft" Quebec industries, Mr. Speaker, they could have given some thought to traditional sectors of the economy. There is a saying in Quebec which goes this way: a healthy construction industry means a healthy provincial economy and they say in the United States: that if the automobile industry is doing well, so is the U.S. economy

May 26, 1978
Income Tax Act
as a whole. And the same can be said about Canada particularly in my own area as we have also 3,000 people working for General Motors in Ste. Therese a few miles south of my riding, and they are not favoured by that 3 percent cut either, and I wonder, Mr. Speaker, when they will go to Quebec requesting a sales tax cut on their products. If workers who feel they have been hurt by this new 5 percent tax levy can demonstrate to voice their discontent, surely workers who have been overlooked in the sales tax cut can do likewise in fact, I invite the employees in the General Motors' plant in Ste. Therese to demonstrate and demand from their provincial government the national programme that has been proposed and was accepted by all other provinces. Other provincial Finance ministers have understood the situation and realized that the recommandation made by C.D. Howe Institute and others was certainly the best way to boost the economy.
It is said that the textile industry was a weak sector in the province of Quebec. According to the data provided by one of the main textile industries in the province of Quebec, the Dominion Textile Ltee., for the third quarter of 1977, their sales have reached $145,700,000. which represents a $406,000,000 increase for the nine first months of the previous year, or a 12 percent increase over the previous year. And those figures, Mr. Speaker, were released on and apply to their 1977 financial year, long before Parizeau proposed his new fiscal policy. So it is no longer a soft sector and these higher sales are certainly due to the measures taken by the Canadian government in 1977 in imposing quotas on the importations of textiles. It is therefore wrong to state that the textile industry is part of the soft sector. Perhaps some industries in the textile field can say they are in a weak sector, but this is surely not true of most of the thriving textile industry of the province of Quebec which has hired additional employees during the last eight or ten months and has increased the volume of its sales. That is obvious in the report submitted by the Dominion Textile Company.
Of course, since November 1976, the economy of the province of Quebec is going down and it is normal. I mentioned earlier an industry which should have been helped by a tax rebate, that is the Quebec building industry because since 1976 generally speaking there has been a slowdown of at least 75 per cent in that industry. I want to emphasize that is was 75 per cent, Mr. Speaker, because the media, especially those from the province of Quebec tend to censure what we say in this House. This is why sometimes we have to repeat to be sure we are understood. There was a 40 per cent decrease compared with last year, that's 1977, and this is very serious. The point, Mr. Speaker is not to find amusing formulas, window-dressing formulas such as the 8 per cent tax rebate on hotel rooms to stimulate this sector of our economy. While I am on the subject Mr. Speaker, it is rather amazing to note that every-time the question of helping the poor comes up in the province of Quebec, it is always the wealthy who do bring it up. The 8

per cent tax on hotel rooms was taken off because, once again, this notorious Finance Minister found out that the minimum living wages in his province, which are unique in Canada and in the rest of the world, have a tremendous detrimental effect on the Quebec tourist industry. To such a degree, Mr. Speaker, that in certain areas of the province, such as Montreal and Quebec City hotels suffered losses of 60 per cent over 1966 and 35 to 40 per cent from 1976 to 1977, which has meant that major hotels in Montreal have had only a 45 per cent occupation rate in 1977 whereas to be profitable, a hotel which wants to give a good service must have at least a 75 per cent occupation rate.
Because of all the requirements imposed upon the Quebec tourist industry because of the minimum living wages which are much higher than the minimum wages of all other areas of North America-in many cases they are at least twice as high-and also because of the tax burden placed upon the tourist industry, we could read in a recent newspaper report published last Monday or Tuesday, that the tax burden per room in the province of Quebec, in Montreal, is around $1,835 whereas in certain tourism oriented areas of the country, it is about $400. There is therefore no need to be an economic expert to see that the Quebec industry is not able to compete with the tourist industry outside Quebec. It is probably for this reason that the provincial minister decided to help once again the poor and reduce the tax of 8 per cent. This will perhaps convince certain members of the provincial cabinet to spend their 1978 summer vacations in Quebec rather than in Old Orchard or somewhere.
However, Mr. Speaker, the impact that such a tax reduction might have will not be felt for a few years yet because it is mostly aimed at the convention industry which can fill the major hotels for three or four days and bring in people who spend an average of $75 to $100 each outside of hotel charges, of course. There are the people at whom the reduction is aimed. Those are the people who have been chased away by our minimum living wages of over $3 in Quebec, which is twice as much as in many other provinces. Those are the people we want to get back. This will not be possible before a couple of years, because such arrangements are always made 18 to 36 months ahead of time. For instance, the conventions which were not held in Quebec this year were cancelled in the spring of 1977 and in the fall of 1976. The stimulating effect we had anticipated with our 3 per cent tax reduction for the whole economy, for all products manufactured in Canada, would indeed have had an immediate effect far more important than reducing the tax on hotel rooms.
Then, Mr. Speaker, tax is removed on shoes. I believe we all want to get the highest salary possible for our work. On the other hand when you need things such as are manufactured in this country, you go out and buy products manufactured abroad, and this is true concerning shoes, since 40 or 50 per

cent of all shoes sold in Quebec are manufactured not in Canada but in other countries specially in Europe.
Practically the same, Mr. Speaker, may be said concerning electrical appliances. Our manufacturers are not better off with Mr. Parizeau's tax reduction. He should have moved in favour of those industries as that sector has lost the greatest number of jobs because European and Japanese products are more competitive. We should improve employment in this industry where wages are quite high. With respect to textiles, that industry did not develop so well, even though it is not true for the whole of the industry, but certain areas of that industry have failed to remodel or automate their facilities as fast as was done elsewhere and wages did not follow the general trend in Canada. Mr. Speaker, that sector should have been helped instead of the shoe industry, for instance, because a high percentage of those products are not manufactured in the province of Quebec.
The same applies to all appliances, washing machines, dryers, and also carpeting, Mr. Speaker. There is a carpet manufacture in my riding and as I said earlier, the workers in that plant are simply insulted because they cannot benefit from that sales tax reduction. Once again, I wonder why the union has not yet staged a demonstration to show that they disagree with the economic policy of the government of the province of Quebec.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it is my firm belief that it is economically unsound to think that it is possible to put the economy back on its feet by favouring one, two, three or even four individual industries. When the industrial incentive program was developed, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion just about ignored sectorial industries and gave special assistance to the development of certain geographical areas and it is rather along that line that Quebec should have taken action.
If there were a proposal to be made, if for some reason the Quebec government wanted to encourage the industrial community in the province, they should have offered a proposal, they should have first responded to the proposal made by our Minister of Finance and suggested that some of the provisions in the program be made applicable in some areas of the province rather than in some others, or that some areas be excluded from the program, and not have discriminated against certain industries. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I say this here, as I would do elsewhere, and this is the place to do so, I support without reserve the provisions included in the budget which the Minister of Finance has brought forward and I hope that the media will play the role which morally is theirs. I am referring especially to those in the province of Quebec which will consider the proposal made by the Minister of Finance, the national proposition, before it is too late. Because, on the one hand, Mr. Speaker, one cannot try to make the people of the province of Quebec believe in sovereignty-association and pretend to be open to any proposal or any offer, and on the

Those people do not seem to realize that they lose all credibility and that all they deserve is the scorn of business circles in the province of Quebec towards an administration as clumsy and as unhealthy for the economy of the province.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow me a question?
